highlights.text: I think of agency as the capacity to both see and act on degrees of freedom that other people overlook. It’s being able to see choices where others only see constraints—the hidden doors in the walls of life. It’s also the courage to walk through those doors, to defy the forces keeping us normal—the pressures imposed by our inner script and by the boxes other people put us in.

Rather than avoiding failure and rejection, agentic people see these as the inevitable costs of personal progress, and opportunities for learning. Rather than assuming that everything worthwhile has been done already, they assume that many great ventures are postponed out of inertia and fear. Rather than taking it for granted that the experts have it under control, they expect that something more can be done, and that they can be the ones to do it. They choose to believe that everything is learnable, even traits and skills often believed to be innate, like charisma or curiosity. And, fundamentally, they take responsibility. They act on the world, rather than the world acting on them.

Anytime you find yourself in the enviable position of actually knowing what you want out of life, you’re allowed to skip all the artificial steps standing between you and it and work on your goal as directly as possible, doing only what matters to advance the plot.

Agency entails the ability to recognize all the degrees of freedom one has. Addiction strips them away, reduces life to one option, and subordinates everything else in service of making sure that option is selected over and over again. To some extent, you can think of addiction and agency as two sets of labels on the same dial, like hot and cold on a tap. Addiction is automaticity. Agency is autonomy.

The exertion of willpower makes you feel like you’re trying. But the feeling of effort doesn’t mean that you’re Actually Trying. Perhaps relationships feel hard for you, so it’s tempting to believe that you’re Actually Trying, that you’ve brought the full weight of your genius to bear on the problem. You might even take some pride in the struggle. Like rigid posture, the strain feels like correctness. But struggling is not evidence that you’ve tried everything. To the contrary, the continuous need for willpower may be the sign of a badly engineered life.

The human default is to voluntarily accept constraints, convincing ourselves that they are mandatory. We choose to accept a set of expectations placed on us by others—or that we imagine others are placing on us. Then, we act as if we’re stuck indefinitely. We all forget our radical freedom as human beings, forget that the list of things we actually have to do is minuscule.
“What consequences am I trying to prevent by living in a way I don’t like?”

Are you currently doing something that is doomed to fail? If so, why aren’t you adjusting your approach? Do you actually want to fail, because that would be more socially acceptable than just quitting, or more comfortable than radically changing the way you’re going about it?

Instant gratification isn’t guaranteed, of course. The only thing you are guaranteed, if you stare into the abyss, is the dignity of living in alignment with the truth, and relief from the grinding dissatisfaction of trying to maintain a fantasy.

Staring into the abyss isn’t a onetime event; it’s a skill that you can return to. And I think you will find that it gets easier with time and practice. When you master this skill, you delight in asking difficult questions. You habitually probe your thinking, challenging yourself to look in directions you might be tempted to avoid. I see this discipline most often in successful startup founders I know, who live in a state of productive paranoia where they test and retest their fundamental assumptions, always mindful of risks that could destroy their enterprise.

I can’t tell you whether staring into your own personal abyss will result in obvious, tangible rewards. What I can tell you is that I know what it looks like when people never attempt it. Sometimes it looks like a hollow life of resentment, trudging through a job you don’t care about, sustainably self-medicating so you don’t have to pay attention to your sadness. Sometimes it looks like bitter complacency in old age, resigning yourself to inauthentic relationships and regret. It’s easy to end up in a place like that, just by consistently avoiding your lurking intuition that something’s wrong.

Imagine you’ve been parachuted1 into your present life as a stranger. Whoever was here before you certainly made a mess of things, but now someone more capable is here to take over. Using the resources available, how can you, the crisis manager, get to work on improving the situation? When you’re messing your life up, the crisis manager is superior to your normal brain. It’s not worrying about sunk costs or wedded to your old processes. The crisis manager throws away the old to-do list and simply asks, “What is the most important priority, and what is the next thing required to achieve it?”

It’s my experience that movie logic is endemic in dysfunctional organizations, friendships, and marriages. People prefer to take cover in a haze of denial and hope that somehow problems will just disappear. Far too often, we allow frustration or anger to intensify until we reach the boiling point and the problem can’t possibly be ignored anymore, instead of naming it well before it becomes critical. Or worse, we might resign ourselves to living with the problem forever by convincing ourselves there’s nothing we can do about it.

As we get older, our lives become increasingly routine, if we let them. We get more constrained and repetitive in our actions, and, as a result, our days become less stimulating. We barely notice life happening because we become so good at walking the Path of Least Embarrassment. But when you tackle a new challenge, you may find yourself in a state of heightened awareness, with brighter colors and sharper lines. You’ve reentered the state of childlike wonder where you don’t have adult concepts to mediate reality, what William James called “blooming, buzzing confusion.”

The high-agency mindset about rejection1 takes things even further. It says that you should seek out rejection, or at least welcome it. Congratulate yourself on hearing no. Remind yourself that if you don’t routinely encounter rejection, you are not asking for enough—you’re only making requests that are extremely likely to receive a yes. By making bolder requests, you will sometimes achieve big leaps, and you’ll know you’re not leaving opportunities on the table.

When I told myself I was “being authentic” by remaining aloof, I was also avoiding having to look at some free-floating shame about my social awkwardness. When you spot an inner defense like this—a reaction of “I can’t do that, it wouldn’t be authentic”—it’s a yellow flag that you’ve noticed a possible area of improvement that you’re avoiding because it’s threatening to your ego.

Some people hesitate to take shortcuts because they disdain the whole idea of taking the easy route. This position is something like: Life is about dealing with complex, thorny problems. If you take all the chores out of your life, all the strain and difficulty, some of the humanness goes out of your existence. We’re meant to weed the soil, to write the thank-you note, to have unnecessary conversations. I absolutely agree with this. My vision of a good life isn’t one where I’m some sort of disembodied switchboard, just routing ideas and decisions around. However, I want to have a choice about the complexity I am spending time with. I want to use my brainpower to tackle the thorny problems that really inspire me, to play the role in the giant human ecosystem that I can play best while leaving others with their ideal labor.

One distinguishing feature5 I’ve noticed among people who are successful is that they just try a lot of stuff—socially, intellectually, professionally. It’s the rate of experimentation, the number of shots on goal6, that provides the magic, not the percentage of successes, which might be very low at first. Conversely, people who move more slowly through life, and achieve less, tend to take fewer shots on goal and have longer feedback loops. Perhaps they work privately on creative projects they don’t show anybody for months or years, or they stay in a relatively contained peer group for a long time without mixing it up.

The winning move here is to start behaving like that chef when you’re just a cook. To assume that you’re aiming for a future that will hold you to a much higher standard, even if you’re not currently held to that standard. People who behave like this—who perform as if they are already an admired success in their field—have a funny way of ending up there. Meanwhile, when you half-ass everything in your life because you’re waiting for a great opportunity to showcase your genius, pretty much nobody thinks, “There goes a latent genius.” Instead, they think, “Ah, there’s a person who likes to half-ass it.” It’s not that every excess outlay of effort pays dividends immediately; it’s that people really notice when you show up despite it not being a matter of duty or obviously in your self-interest. And people remember it.

Who’s Melvin? It’s a part of the human personality that exists in all of us, the part that’s good at avoiding blame or embarrassment by “acting normal.” Melvin is always taking the reasonable approach: Faced with a dilemma at work, rather than striving to really tackle it, Melvin executes a normal-shaped, solution-type action-thing. You know the old saying “Nobody gets fired for buying IBM?” Melvin is the part of us that, faced with a big, chewy problem, tries to buy IBM—to do something that might not be maximally effective but that won’t get you criticized. And then, if that doesn’t work, Melvin assumes the problem is unsolvable, then stops.

Often, when we play the Melvin game, we’re attempting to satisfy both our aspirational self, which desires a meaningful, complex existence, and our timid self, which wants us to be left alone in our cozy little blame-free corner. The issue here is that you can’t satisfy both selves at once. You typically have to pick either the scary goal of really wanting to do things or the comforting goal of hanging on to safety.

Really wanting something is a stressful experience. When we allow ourselves to fully want, we create a sense of incompleteness in our world, which hovers over us until we get it, or fail conclusively. And, since any of our efforts might fail for reasons beyond our control, by really wanting something, we are signing up for potential heartbreak. Often adding to the fear of our own heartbreak is the dread that we’ll be seen as a failure by others.

Assume you will achieve your goal, even if it requires multiple attempts. Take it on faith that the world is more pliable than feels true. Refuse to accept your brain’s first-order response that you probably can’t achieve goal X because of restrictions Y and Z. Instead, approach restrictions Y and Z with a puzzle-solving mindset, relishing the challenge of discovering how to work around them.

Don’t let Melvin deceive you. Rebel against what you see as the limits of reality and you’ll find that reality tends to be quite malleable. The real boundaries are typically beyond the constraints of our imagination when we’re tired or afraid; they’re certainly beyond Melvin’s.

The delusion is that commitment is a matter of feeling committed—that you are committed when you dwell in a state of emotional conviction so durable that you won’t ever waver from it in the future. You’re committed when you know in your heart that you’ll never cheat on your spouse, or abandon writing your book, or take money from an investor who’s not really mission-aligned. This is a delusion because we’re simply not capable of such emotional steadfastness. Emotions are too variable. If we’re counting on maintaining an emotional state all the way through a long-term course of challenging action, we’re completely doomed.

A commitment accompanied by the right kind of forcing function can almost magically foster deep focus, resolve, and creativity; truly, “Necessity is the mother of invention.” If you’re only half-committed to an ambitious project, a huge amount of your cognition will be devoted to fantasies of escaping the work, daydreaming about ways out of the discomfort: Wouldn’t it be nice if I could blow this imposing deadline? But when the path to escape is removed, the full force of your ingenuity is directed toward the goal.

People wait to feel committed rather than deciding to make a commitment. But the feeling of commitment doesn’t come easily when both people are exploring other options. If you have an easy off-ramp, you’re less likely to honestly confront your tendencies in the way that grows you into a better partner and creates real intimacy.

Our lives are composed of routines and habits that are leftovers—the solutions we adopted the first or fifth time we were exposed to a problem. We’re often stuck mentally with whatever constraints, of resources or imagination, we had at that earlier time.

In these moments, what is important is a specific kind of agency: opportunism—the sensitivity to notice that a potential diversion from your life’s path has presented itself, the inventiveness to come up with a way of pursuing it, and the courage to say, “Hey, what’s the worst that could happen?” People who are successfully opportunistic take big leaps that make them progressively more alive.
